prompt: You are the test author this time: write isCorrect so it accepts a correct Rotator and rejects broken ones. Complete the checker in the starter file, then run the tests.
explanation: Two of these bugs are invisible to a single happy-path call. Rotating {1,2,3,4,5} by 2 and rotating it by 5-and-something look identical unless you deliberately pass a k larger than the array, and an implementation that rotates the caller's array in place returns exactly the right contents -- the only way to catch it is to keep a reference to the array you passed in and check afterwards that it is untouched. The empty array is the boundary where `k % n` divides by zero, so a checker that does not try it will certify a program that crashes on the first empty input it meets.
hints: Compare arrays with java.util.Arrays.equals, not ==. Two different arrays holding the same numbers are not the same object.
Pass a k that is bigger than the array (say k = 5 on a 3-element array) -- one broken implementation only fails there.
Keep your own reference to the array you passed in, and after the call check it still holds what it did before: the contract says a NEW array comes back.
